title: Welcome
hook: blessings and visits greet a new baby

segments.voice: Yesterday we opened a new block, and your line was a life has rituals. Which stage of your own life was marked, and which slipped by unmarked? Today, the very first stage. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

Bethlehem, at the end of the book of Ruth. A baby boy has just been born to Ruth and Boaz. And the scene the book chooses to show us is not the birth. It's the neighbors. The women of the town crowd around Naomi, the grandmother, the one who came home bitter and empty-handed. They bless God for her. They tell her this child will restore her life and care for her when she's old. Naomi takes the baby and holds him to her chest. And then the women do one more thing: they give him his name, Obed. A child arrives, and the street shows up. Today's word is what they were doing.
screen: `A BABY IN BETHLEHEM.` → `THE NEIGHBORS CROWD IN.` → `THEY BLESS, AND THEY NAME HIM.`

segments.voice: Welcome. Turn it four ways. First, a blessing for good news. Jewish tradition gives words for moments of joy. The Talmud teaches that on hearing good news that brings good to others as well as to you, you bless God as the one who is good and does good. Some authorities apply it to the birth of a child, a joy the whole household shares. Before the baby has done anything, the first response is gratitude. Second, the visit. In Ashkenazi custom, on the first Friday night after a boy is born, friends come to the family's home for a gathering called shalom zachar, welcome to the male. There are snacks, songs, words of Torah. Sephardi and other communities have their own customs, and families welcome girls with gatherings too, which we'll meet later this week. The point is the same: nobody greets a new life alone. Third, the words at the door. When a baby is carried in to a ceremony, people often call out baruch haba, blessed is the one who comes. It echoes a line from the Psalms, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the LORD." Fourth, back to Bethlehem. The women in Ruth don't just congratulate. They speak about the baby's future and about Naomi's healing. Welcome, in that story, is a promise: we see this child, and we see the family around him.
screen: `GOOD NEWS GETS A BLESSING.` · `FRIENDS COME ON FRIDAY NIGHT.` · `BLESSED IS THE ONE WHO COMES.` · `THE NEIGHBORS SPEAK A FUTURE.` · then, large: `WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless a new baby. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a baby you know, or have heard about, or one due soon. If no baby comes to mind, choose any newcomer: a new neighbor, a new coworker, a new pet. Picture their face, or just their name. Now say, inside, the words from the Psalm: blessed is the one who comes. Then add one good thing you hope for them. Not advice. A hope. If you pray, you can hold that child in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Welcome. The blessing for good news, the friends who come to the house, and baruch haba at the door. Today's word.
Your line: welcome. Today, greet one newcomer out loud: a baby, a new face at work, someone who just moved in. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: When a Jewish baby is born, families often recite a blessing of thanks, and in many communities friends gather at the home, such as at a shalom zachar, an Ashkenazi custom on the first Friday night after a boy's birth.

notes: Psalms 118:26 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.

Berakhot 59b (hatov vehametiv for good news shared with others) paraphrased; application to the birth of a child attributed to 'some authorities' (cf. Berakhot 59b on a wife giving birth to a son, and later codes). Confirm phrasing and whether to mention the birth of a daughter.

Shalom zachar described as a custom 'in many Ashkenazi communities' on the first Friday night after a boy's birth; confirm. 'Sephardi and other communities have their own nights and customs' kept general on purpose.
Ruth 4:13–17 paraphrased: the women bless God, say the child will restore Naomi's life, Naomi nurses/holds him, the women name him Obed. Confirm 'holds him to her chest' as a fair rendering of 4:16.
baruch haba as the greeting when a baby is brought in (e.g. at a brit); stated as 'often'. Confirm.
